## scrivener/binder

A Scrivener project's binder, and the names of its styles.

The binder is the `.scrivx` file at the top of the project: XML, each item
a `BinderItem` with its id, its type, its title and the items under it. An
item's own files are kept under `Files/Data/<id>/`, which is how the rest of
the import finds its text. The Trash is left out here, so nothing after this
sees it.

The styles are `Files/styles.xml`, each with an id and a name. A text lists
the ids of the styles it uses, and its markers number them in that order.

## BinderItem

An item in the binder.

Type: [Object][160]

### Properties

- `id` **[string][161]** Its UUID, which names the folder its files are in
- `type` **[string][161]** Scrivener's own: `DraftFolder`, `ResearchFolder`,
  `Folder`, `Text`, `PDF`, `Image`, …
- `title` **[string][161]** As written; empty for an untitled item
- `extension` **[string][161]?** A file's, from the item's metadata
- `children` **[Array][162]<[BinderItem][2]>**&#x20;

## scrivener

A Scrivener 3 project brought into a project: the binder as the
tree, each text as markdown, and the files in Research as file documents.

The project comes in as a `.scriv` chosen under Projects › Import project…,
which the browser hands over zipped, or a zip of one, and makes a new
project; or dropped or chosen in a folder of the tree, where it lands as a
folder named after it. Either way it
is opened and checked before anything is written. What markdown cannot hold
is left behind: fonts and the rest of the formatting, labels, keywords,
snapshots, compile settings. Comments, footnotes, links and pictures in the
text are not read yet, for want of a project that has them to test against.

- **package** - A project's files by their path inside it, from a folder or
  a zip
- **binder** - The binder read from the `.scrivx`, without the Trash, and
  the styles' names
- **rtf** - A text's RTF read into paragraphs and tables, with Scrivener's
  style markers taken out
- **markdown** - Those written as markdown, through the editor's schema and
  serializer
- **project** - A project opened, then written into the tree

`npm run scrivener` runs the reading over a project on disk and prints what
would come in. Design: `.llm/scrivener_import_design.md`.

### Examples

```javascript
import { packageOfZip } from '@/scrivener/package.js'
import { openProject, writeProject } from '@/scrivener/project.js'

const pack = await packageOfZip(file)
if (pack) await writeProject(storyId, await openProject(pack), { asFolder: true })
```

## scrivener/markdown

What was read out of a Scrivener text, written as markdown.

The paragraphs and tables are built into a document in the editor's schema
and written out by the editor's serializer, so the markdown is in the file
format's own form and its escaping is the serializer's: a scene break typed
as a lone `#` stays a `#`, not an empty heading.

Scrivener's paragraph styles are known by name. Title is a heading of the
first level and Heading n one of level n + 1, so a Title keeps its place
above the Heading 1s under it; Block Quote is a block quote and Code Block a
code block. Any other style is an ordinary paragraph. Lists nest by level,
and a level that jumps more than one deeper than the item before it is
taken as one deeper. Empty paragraphs, which lay out space in Scrivener,
are dropped.

A table of one row lays out a page rather than holding data, as the title
page in Scrivener's novel template does: its cells are paragraphs, their
lines kept. A longer one is a table, its first row the header, a cell's
lines run together, since a cell holds one.

## scrivener/package

A Scrivener project's files, by their path inside it, from a
folder or a zip.

A project is a folder named `<name>.scriv`, which a Mac shows as one file.
It comes in dropped, as a folder with its files listed, or zipped: by
Finder's Compress, by Scrivener's backups, or by the browser. Chrome and
Electron zip a package chosen in a file chooser, as a Mac shows it, and hand
it over as `<name>.scriv.zip`. Either way what the import gets is the same:
the project's name, and its files by their path under the `.scriv`, the
binder (`<name>.scrivx`) among them at the top.

A zip is listed before anything in it is unpacked, so asking whether one
holds a project costs only its directory, and only the project's own files
are unpacked: not the `__MACOSX` folder Finder adds, nor anything beside the
project.

## ScrivenerPackage

Type: [Object][160]

### Properties

- `name` **[string][161]** The project's: its `.scriv` folder's name without
  the extension
- `files` **[Map][167]<[string][161], [Blob][171]>** Every file in it, by its path inside
  it, `/`-separated

## scrivener/project

A Scrivener project opened, then written into a project's tree.

Opening reads the binder and the styles and checks that there is a project
to import, so that a zip with none in it, or a project too old to read,
writes nothing. Writing then goes through the binder in order:

- A folder is an ordered folder, since the binder's order is the
  writer's. When it has text of its own, that comes first inside it, as a
  document of the same name.
- A text is a text document, empty or not: an empty scene in the binder is
  a plan.
- A file, such as a PDF or a picture in Research, is a file document, read
  as any import reads it. One that cannot be read comes in with no text
  rather than being left out.
- A text or a file with items under it is that document, holding them in
  the binder's order (`.llm/nested_documents_design.md`).
- An item's synopsis and notes are documents of their own, `<title>
synopsis` and `<title> notes`, right after its text: beside a document
  with nothing under it, or inside a folder or a document before the items
  under it.

Labels, statuses, keywords, snapshots, compile settings and the rest of
what Scrivener keeps about its items have nowhere to go, and are left.

## scrivener/rtf

A Scrivener text's RTF, read into paragraphs and tables.

Scrivener on a Mac writes its RTF through macOS's text system, which uses a
small and regular part of the format: a font table, a color table and a
list table, then the paragraphs, each opened by `\pard` and its settings
and closed by a backslash at the end of a line. What a markdown document can
hold is kept: bold, italic and strikethrough, which list a paragraph is in
and how deep, which of Scrivener's paragraph styles it is in, and tables, as
the text in their cells. Fonts, sizes, colors, spacing and the rest are read
past.

Scrivener marks its styles in the text itself: `<$Scr_Ps::0>` opens the
first of the styles the text uses, `<!$Scr_Ps::0>` closes it, and the
paragraphs between are in it. The markers come out here, and each paragraph
keeps the name of the style it was in.

Anything else is read as the text it holds, and what holds none, such as a
picture's data or a field's instruction, is dropped. Nothing in the content
throws.

## Run

a `\n` in it.
